title: The ban
hookLine: Antiochus IV outlaws Torah practice and defiles the Temple
tomorrow: The mother and seven sons (2 Maccabees 7)
last: SOMETHING ALWAYS STAYS BEHIND IN THE ORIGINAL.

cards: The order arrives in writing. The first book of Maccabees says the king, Antiochus, the one surnamed Epiphanes, writes to his whole kingdom that everyone should be one people, and each should give up their own laws.
Then letters go to Jerusalem and the towns of Judah, with a list. No more offerings in the Temple. No Sabbaths or festivals.
No circumcising sons. Eat what the law forbids. And at the bottom, the penalty: whoever will not obey shall die.
Officers are sent to make sure. For a family in a village in Judah, keeping the Sabbath in their own home was now a crime.

teach.b: The book doesn't soften anything. On the Temple altar, the king's men set up what the King James text calls "the abomination of desolation", an idol's altar where the altar of God had stood.
Copies of the books of the law are torn to pieces and burned. Women who circumcised their babies are put to death. And the book is honest that this pressure split the people.

Many in Israel went along, offered to idols and broke the Sabbath. Many others refused and would not eat what the law forbade, even when refusing meant dying. Both groups were Jews, under the same pressure.
This is not a story of good nations and bad nations. It's what happens when a government decides that one way of life has to disappear.
The rabbis later had a word for that kind of time: shmad, a time when practicing at all is forbidden.

The Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, teaches that in an ordinary time a person may break many commandments to save a life, but when a ruling power decrees against the faith, even a small custom becomes a line not to cross.
One teacher's example is as small as changing a shoe strap. Next come a mother and her sons, a priest in a small town who says no, and the holiday that grew out of it all.

how: Jews remember the persecution under Antiochus at Hanukkah, when the Al HaNissim passage in the prayers recalls a wicked Greek kingdom that tried to make Israel forget the Torah.

o: a boycott on trading with Greek merchants in Jerusalem
a Temple rule keeping foreigners out of its courts

games.q: you're a parent in a village in Judah. the king's officers say: no Sabbath, no circumcision, or die. what does the text say people did?
o: some went along, and many others refused, even unto death.
games.why: 1 Maccabees is honest that the pressure split the people: many went along, and many others held firm and chose to die rather than break the covenant.

practice: Think of one thing you're free to do because of what you believe or where you come from, light a candle, rest on a certain day, or choose no practice at all, and imagine a letter arriving that forbids it.
Then let it go, notice that no such letter came, and spare a thought for anyone, of any faith, who did get one. If you pray, use words from your own tradition for them.

wordCard.voice: The ban. A king's written order outlawing Sabbath, circumcision and Torah, and an idol set on the Temple altar. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the rabbis' word for a time of persecution, when practicing the faith itself is forbidden.

carryVoice: Your line: freedom to practice. Under that king, it cost some people everything. Day eight hundred ninety, done.
